_meta.source: single source of truth for test definitions

tests.name: Hemoglobin
tests.explanation_low: Your hemoglobin level is below the normal range, which is often associated with anemia. This can reduce oxygen delivery throughout the body, causing fatigue, weakness, or shortness of breath. It is recommended to discuss dietary iron intake or potential underlying causes with your doctor.
tests.explanation_high: Your hemoglobin level is above the normal range, which can indicate polycythemia or dehydration. It means your blood has a higher concentration of red blood cells, making it thicker. This can sometimes be related to low oxygen levels, smoking, or bone marrow issues, so consulting your physician is advised.

tests.name: White Blood Cell Count
tests.explanation_low: A low white blood cell count, or leukopenia, suggests that your body has a reduced capacity to fight off infections. This can be caused by viral infections, autoimmune conditions, bone marrow issues, or certain medications. You should take precautions to avoid illnesses and seek medical guidance.
tests.explanation_high: An elevated white blood cell count, or leukocytosis, is typically a sign that your body is responding to an infection, inflammation, or physical stress. It can also be triggered by certain medications or bone marrow conditions. A medical professional can help identify the source of the immune response.

tests.name: Platelet Count
tests.explanation_low: A low platelet count, known as thrombocytopenia, can impair your blood’s ability to clot effectively. This might increase your risk of bruising easily or bleeding from minor cuts. It is important to avoid activities that could cause injury and consult your doctor for further evaluation.
tests.explanation_high: A high platelet count, or thrombocytosis, means your body is producing too many platelets, which can sometimes increase the risk of blood clots. This can be a reaction to inflammation, infection, or a primary bone marrow disorder. A doctor can help determine the underlying trigger.

tests.name: Red Blood Cell Count
tests.explanation_low: A low red blood cell count, or anemia, means your body is producing fewer oxygen-carrying cells than normal. This can lead to tiredness, pale skin, or dizziness as tissues receive less oxygen. Discussing dietary adjustments or iron supplements with a doctor is highly beneficial.
tests.explanation_high: An elevated red blood cell count, or erythrocytosis, indicates a higher-than-normal concentration of red cells in your circulation. This can be caused by chronic low oxygen, dehydration, or renal conditions. A physician can help explore the exact cause and recommend any necessary steps.

tests.name: Hematocrit
tests.explanation_low: A low hematocrit level indicates a lower-than-normal proportion of red blood cells in your blood volume, often signaling anemia. This can lead to reduced physical stamina, feeling cold, or fatigue. It is recommended to evaluate iron, folate, or B12 levels with your healthcare provider.
tests.explanation_high: A high hematocrit level means red blood cells make up an abnormally large percentage of your blood, which is very common in cases of dehydration. It can also point to conditions that cause overproduction of red cells. Rehydrating and consulting a doctor can clarify these results.

tests.name: Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)
tests.explanation_low: Low MCV indicates microcytosis, meaning your red blood cells are smaller than average. This is most commonly caused by iron deficiency anemia or thalassemia trait. A physician can order iron studies to verify the cause.
tests.explanation_high: High MCV indicates macrocytosis, meaning your red blood cells are larger than normal. Common reasons include Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, thyroid underactivity, or liver stress. Consulting your doctor is recommended.

tests.name: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)
tests.explanation_low: Low MCH means there is less hemoglobin per red blood cell, giving cells a paler color (hypochromia). It typically accompanies microcytic anemias like iron deficiency.
tests.explanation_high: High MCH indicates a higher amount of hemoglobin per cell, frequently seen in macrocytic anemias associated with B12 or folate deficiency.

tests.name: MCHC
tests.explanation_low: Low MCHC indicates a low hemoglobin concentration relative to red cell volume, often seen in severe iron deficiency anemia or hemoglobinopathies.
tests.explanation_high: High MCHC indicates an abnormally concentrated hemoglobin within red cells, which can occur in hereditary spherocytosis, severe burn injuries, or autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

tests.name: Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW)
tests.explanation_low: Low RDW indicates that red blood cells are highly uniform in size, which is generally a healthy finding and rarely clinically significant.
tests.explanation_high: High RDW indicates significant variation in red blood cell size (anisocytosis), often an early indicator of mixed nutritional deficiencies or evolving anemia.

tests.name: Neutrophils
tests.explanation_low: Low neutrophil percentage (neutropenia) weakens the primary defense against bacterial infections, potentially caused by viral illnesses, autoimmune disorders, or bone marrow suppression.
tests.explanation_high: High neutrophil percentage (neutrophilia) is typically an acute immune response to bacterial infection, systemic tissue inflammation, or severe physiological stress.

tests.name: Total Cholesterol
tests.explanation_low: Low total cholesterol levels can occasionally be linked to hyperthyroidism, liver disease, malabsorption, or malnutrition. While high cholesterol is a more common concern, extremely low levels also merit a medical review to ensure there are no underlying metabolic issues.
tests.explanation_high: High total cholesterol indicates elevated levels of fats in your bloodstream, which can increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. It is often influenced by diet, physical activity levels, genetics, or metabolic conditions. Lifestyle modifications and medical consultation are standard next steps.

tests.name: LDL Cholesterol
tests.explanation_low: Low LDL cholesterol, sometimes referred to as "bad" cholesterol, is generally favorable for heart health but can occasionally be associated with malnutrition, genetic factors, or an overactive thyroid. A doctor can review this in the context of your overall health profile.
tests.explanation_high: High LDL cholesterol is associated with plaque buildup in your arteries, raising the risk of heart disease or stroke. It is highly responsive to dietary changes, aerobic exercise, and in some cases, cholesterol-lowering medications. Discussing a management plan with your doctor is advised.

tests.name: HDL Cholesterol
tests.explanation_low: Low HDL cholesterol, the "good" cholesterol, reduces your body’s natural ability to clear excess fats from your bloodstream, which can increase cardiovascular risk. Factors like smoking, obesity, and inactivity contribute to low HDL. Increasing physical activity can help raise these levels.
tests.explanation_high: High HDL cholesterol is generally protective against heart disease as it helps clear other forms of cholesterol from your bloodstream. However, extremely high levels can occasionally indicate metabolic or genetic variations. It is best reviewed as part of a complete cardiovascular assessment.

tests.name: Triglycerides
tests.explanation_low: Low triglyceride levels are relatively rare but can indicate low-fat diets, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption syndromes, or overall malnutrition. If other lipids are normal, it is typically not an immediate concern, but a doctor can provide a comprehensive interpretation.
tests.explanation_high: High triglycerides represent an elevated level of storage fat in your blood, which can contribute to the hardening of arteries or pancreatitis. This is often linked to high-carbohydrate diets, alcohol consumption, sedentary lifestyle, or poorly controlled diabetes. Consulting a physician is recommended.

tests.name: VLDL Cholesterol
tests.explanation_low: Low VLDL cholesterol levels are generally considered beneficial and indicate low circulating levels of triglyceride-rich particles.
tests.explanation_high: High VLDL cholesterol carries triglycerides throughout the bloodstream, and elevated levels contribute to arterial plaque accumulation and metabolic syndrome.

tests.name: Non-HDL Cholesterol
tests.explanation_low: Low non-HDL cholesterol reflects minimal atherogenic lipoprotein burden in circulation, which is ideal for long-term cardiovascular health.
tests.explanation_high: High non-HDL cholesterol measures total atherogenic lipid burden (LDL + VLDL + IDL) and is a strong predictor of coronary artery disease risk.

tests.name: Total Cholesterol / HDL Ratio
tests.explanation_low: A low Total Cholesterol to HDL ratio indicates a highly protective lipid balance with ample high-density lipoprotein protection.
tests.explanation_high: An elevated Total Cholesterol to HDL ratio suggests an unfavorable balance of circulating fats, increasing overall risk for ischemic heart events.

tests.name: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone
tests.explanation_low: A low TSH level usually suggests that your thyroid gland is overactive, a condition known as hyperthyroidism. This can cause symptoms like weight loss, a rapid heartbeat, anxiety, or heat sensitivity. A physician can help run follow-up thyroid scans or hormone tests.
tests.explanation_high: A high TSH level typically indicates that your thyroid gland is underactive, known as hypothyroidism. This causes your metabolism to slow down, potentially leading to weight gain, fatigue, dry skin, or feeling cold. This is a common and highly treatable condition that a doctor can manage.

tests.name: Triiodothyronine (T3)
tests.explanation_low: Low T3 levels can occur during severe illness, fasting, or as part of hypothyroidism where the thyroid gland is underproducing hormones. This can contribute to sluggishness and low metabolic rate. A medical review of your entire thyroid panel is recommended.
tests.explanation_high: High T3 levels indicate hyperthyroidism, meaning your thyroid gland is producing too much active hormone. This can speed up your metabolism, causing nervousness, hand tremors, or an increased heart rate. A physician can discuss treatments to regulate hormone production.

tests.name: Thyroxine (T4)
tests.explanation_low: Low T4 levels point toward hypothyroidism, where the thyroid does not produce enough hormone to sustain standard metabolic functions. This can cause fatigue, depression, or weight gain. A doctor can guide you on hormone replacement therapies if needed.
tests.explanation_high: High T4 levels are typically a sign of hyperthyroidism, where the thyroid is overproducing hormones. This can lead to excessive energy use, rapid pulse, sweating, or unexpected weight loss. Consulting a healthcare provider is key to finding the right therapy.

tests.name: Free T3
tests.explanation_low: Low Free T3 reflects decreased circulating active thyroid hormone, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, or metabolic slowing.
tests.explanation_high: High Free T3 indicates excessive thyroid activity (hyperthyroidism), driving rapid heart rate, weight loss, or restlessness.

tests.name: Free T4
tests.explanation_low: Low Free T4 indicates primary or secondary thyroid gland underactivity, reducing basic cellular metabolic rate.
tests.explanation_high: High Free T4 confirms active thyroid hormone overproduction, commonly seen in Graves disease or toxic nodular goiter.

tests.name: Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase Antibodies (Anti-TPO)
tests.explanation_low: Low or undetectable Anti-TPO antibodies indicate absence of autoimmune thyroid targeting.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated Anti-TPO antibodies indicate autoimmune thyroiditis (such as Hashimotos or Graves disease), where antibodies target thyroid enzyme tissue.

tests.name: Alanine Transaminase
tests.explanation_low: Low ALT levels are generally normal and expected, representing a healthy liver with minimal cell leakage. In rare cases, extremely low levels can be linked to vitamin B6 deficiency or chronic kidney disease. A standard medical check can confirm if any action is needed.
tests.explanation_high: High ALT levels indicate that liver cells are irritated or damaged, causing this enzyme to leak into your blood. Common causes include fatty liver, alcohol use, certain medications, or viral hepatitis. It is highly recommended to seek medical advice to identify and treat the underlying cause.

tests.name: Aspartate Transaminase
tests.explanation_low: Low AST levels are common and usually indicate a healthy, normal liver function. Very low levels can occasionally be seen in vitamin B6 deficiency or severe renal conditions. A doctor can interpret this in conjunction with your other liver enzymes.
tests.explanation_high: An elevated AST level suggests cellular damage, most commonly in the liver, but sometimes in muscles or the heart. This can be caused by fatty liver disease, heavy alcohol intake, certain medications, or muscle injury. Consulting your physician can help determine the exact source.

tests.name: Total Bilirubin
tests.explanation_low: Low bilirubin levels are generally not a cause for concern and are often considered normal. Some studies suggest it might be linked to high caffeine intake or certain medications, but it does not indicate any liver issues on its own.
tests.explanation_high: High bilirubin levels can cause jaundice, characterized by yellowing of the skin and eyes. This can be due to liver conditions, bile duct blockages, or an increased breakdown of red blood cells. It is important to consult a physician to evaluate your liver and biliary system.

tests.name: Alkaline Phosphatase
tests.explanation_low: Low ALP levels can be related to malnutrition, zinc or magnesium deficiency, hypothyroidism, or a rare genetic disorder called hypophosphatasia. A medical professional can help evaluate your diet and overall metabolic health.
tests.explanation_high: High ALP levels are most frequently associated with liver diseases, bone disorders, or bile duct obstruction. It is also normally elevated in growing children and pregnant women. A doctor can run additional tests to pinpoint whether the source is bone or liver.

tests.name: Direct Bilirubin
tests.explanation_low: Low direct conjugated bilirubin is standard and expected in healthy metabolic processing.
tests.explanation_high: High direct bilirubin indicates impaired bile excretion from the liver or biliary tract obstruction (gallstones or choledocholithiasis).

tests.name: Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT)
tests.explanation_low: Low GGT levels are reassuring and indicate healthy hepatic and biliary tract function.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated GGT is a sensitive marker for liver irritation, biliary stasis, alcohol exposure, or drug-induced hepatotoxicity.

tests.name: Total Serum Protein
tests.explanation_low: Low total protein can reflect liver synthesis impairment, kidney protein loss, or malnutrition.
tests.explanation_high: High total protein can be caused by chronic inflammation, viral infections, dehydration, or bone marrow disorders.

tests.name: Albumin
tests.explanation_low: Low serum albumin suggests reduced liver synthesis capacity, active inflammation, kidney filtration leakage, or severe protein malnutrition.
tests.explanation_high: High albumin is almost exclusively caused by acute intravascular dehydration or severe fluid loss.

tests.name: Creatinine
tests.explanation_low: Low creatinine levels are often linked to low muscle mass, severe weight loss, pregnancy, or a low-protein diet. While not usually dangerous, it suggests your body may have reduced muscle bulk. Discussing your nutrition and activity with a doctor is a good idea.
tests.explanation_high: High creatinine levels suggest that your kidneys are not filtering waste products from your blood as efficiently as they should. This can be caused by dehydration, kidney damage, high protein intake, or certain medications. Consulting a healthcare provider is essential to assess kidney health.

tests.name: Blood Urea Nitrogen
tests.explanation_low: Low BUN levels are uncommon but can occur in cases of overhydration, malnutrition, low-protein diets, or severe liver disease. Your liver produces urea, so low levels can sometimes reflect liver health. A medical evaluation can clarify these findings.
tests.explanation_high: High BUN levels typically mean your kidneys are not clearing urea from your blood effectively, often due to dehydration or decreased kidney function. It can also be elevated by high-protein diets or certain heart conditions. Rehydrating and seeing your doctor can help clarify the cause.

tests.name: Uric Acid
tests.explanation_low: Low uric acid levels are rare and typically harmless, sometimes linked to low-protein diets, liver disease, or a condition called SIADH. If other kidney markers are normal, it is rarely an issue, but a doctor can review your overall metabolic profile.
tests.explanation_high: High uric acid levels can lead to the formation of crystals in the joints, causing a painful inflammatory condition called gout. It can also increase the risk of kidney stones. A physician can help suggest dietary changes or medications to lower uric acid.

tests.name: Estimated GFR (eGFR)
tests.explanation_low: A lower eGFR indicates reduced kidney filtration capacity. Values below 60 warrant clinical evaluation for chronic kidney disease.
tests.explanation_high: Normal or high eGFR demonstrates robust kidney blood filtration rate with no signs of clearance decline.

tests.name: HbA1c
tests.explanation_low: A low HbA1c level is generally rare but can occur in people with certain types of anemia or conditions that shorten red blood cell lifespan. It represents a low average blood sugar over the last three months, which is best reviewed in detail by a doctor.
tests.explanation_high: An elevated HbA1c level indicates higher-than-normal average blood sugar levels over the past 3 months. A value between 5.7% and 6.4% suggests prediabetes, while 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes. It is highly recommended to seek medical advice for proper management.

tests.name: Fasting Blood Sugar
tests.explanation_low: Low fasting blood sugar, or hypoglycemia, indicates your body has insufficient glucose for energy, which can cause shakiness, sweating, dizziness, or confusion. This can be due to fasting, heavy exercise, or diabetes medication. Immediate sugar intake and a medical check are advised.
tests.explanation_high: High fasting blood sugar indicates elevated glucose levels after fasting, which is a major sign of prediabetes or diabetes. It can lead to long-term health complications if left unmanaged. Lifestyle adjustments and consulting a healthcare professional are essential.

tests.name: Postprandial Blood Sugar
tests.explanation_low: Low postprandial glucose suggests reactive hypoglycemia or excessive insulin release following meal digestion.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated postprandial blood sugar (>140 mg/dL) indicates impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes after meal challenge.

tests.name: Fasting Serum Insulin
tests.explanation_low: Low fasting insulin can indicate inadequate pancreatic beta-cell secretion, seen in Type 1 diabetes or late-stage pancreatic fatigue.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated fasting insulin is a classic signal of systemic insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, or early prediabetes compensatory response.

tests.name: Vitamin D
tests.explanation_low: Low vitamin D levels, or deficiency, can weaken bones, cause muscle pain, and lower your immune response. It is very common and can be addressed through sun exposure, vitamin-D rich foods, or oral supplements. Consulting a doctor can help determine the correct dose.
tests.explanation_high: High vitamin D levels, though rare, can lead to hypercalcemia, which is an excess of calcium in the blood. This can cause nausea, weakness, and kidney issues, and is almost always due to taking too many high-dose supplements. Stopping supplements and seeing a doctor is advised.

tests.name: Vitamin B12
tests.explanation_low: A low vitamin B12 level can cause megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms like tingling in the hands and feet, fatigue, or memory difficulties. It is common in vegetarians and older adults and is easily treated with supplements or injections. A doctor can guide your therapy.
tests.explanation_high: An elevated vitamin B12 level is often due to high-dose supplement use and is generally non-toxic as excess is excreted in urine. However, in some cases, extremely high levels without supplementation can be associated with liver disease or myeloid conditions, warranting medical review.

tests.name: Ferritin
tests.explanation_low: Low ferritin levels indicate that your body’s iron stores are depleted, which is the primary cause of iron-deficiency anemia. This can leave you feeling chronically tired, weak, cold, or short of breath. A doctor can recommend dietary changes and safe iron supplements.
tests.explanation_high: High ferritin levels indicate an excess of iron stored in your tissues, which can be due to genetic conditions, liver disease, chronic inflammation, or frequent blood transfusions. It is important to see a healthcare professional to identify the cause and prevent tissue damage.

tests.name: Serum Iron
tests.explanation_low: Low serum iron indicates insufficient circulating iron available for immediate hemoglobin synthesis.
tests.explanation_high: High serum iron can indicate iron overload (hemochromatosis), excessive supplementation, or acute liver injury.

tests.name: Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
tests.explanation_low: Low TIBC occurs in iron overload, malnutrition, or chronic inflammatory illnesses.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated TIBC is a classic compensatory signal indicating iron deficiency, as transferrin production increases to bind scarce iron.

tests.name: Transferrin Saturation
tests.explanation_low: Low transferrin saturation (<20%) confirms iron deficiency anemia or impaired iron delivery for blood cell creation.
tests.explanation_high: High transferrin saturation (>50%) warns of systemic iron overload, risking tissue damage in organs like the liver and heart.

tests.name: Folate (Vitamin B9)
tests.explanation_low: Low folate causes megaloblastic anemia, neural tube risks during pregnancy, and fatigue.
tests.explanation_high: High folate is usually harmless and related to diet or vitamin fortification.

tests.name: Sodium (Na)
tests.explanation_low: Low sodium (hyponatremia) can cause headache, confusion, muscle weakness, or seizures, often due to fluid retention or diuretic use.
tests.explanation_high: High sodium (hypernatremia) indicates fluid deficit, severe dehydration, or excessive salt consumption.

tests.name: Potassium (K)
tests.explanation_low: Low potassium (hypokalemia) causes muscle cramps, weakness, fatigue, and potential cardiac arrhythmia.
tests.explanation_high: High potassium (hyperkalemia) is a critical cardiac risk that requires medical attention to prevent heart rhythm complications.

tests.name: Chloride (Cl)
tests.explanation_low: Low chloride (hypochloremia) can be caused by prolonged vomiting, heart failure, or metabolic alkalosis.
tests.explanation_high: High chloride (hyperchloremia) can indicate dehydration, kidney disease, or metabolic acidosis.

tests.name: Calcium (Ca)
tests.explanation_low: Low calcium (hypocalcemia) can cause muscle spasms, numbness in fingers, or bone thinning.
tests.explanation_high: High calcium (hypercalcemia) can cause nausea, kidney stones, and bone pain, often linked to hyperparathyroidism or high vitamin D.

tests.name: Phosphorus (P)
tests.explanation_low: Low phosphorus (hypophosphatemia) can cause muscle weakness, bone pain, and fatigue.
tests.explanation_high: High phosphorus (hyperphosphatemia) is commonly associated with chronic kidney disease or hypoparathyroidism.

tests.name: Magnesium (Mg)
tests.explanation_low: Low magnesium (hypomagnesemia) leads to muscle twitching, tremors, cramps, and cardiac irregularities.
tests.explanation_high: High magnesium (hypermagnesemia) can cause low blood pressure, lethargy, and impaired reflexes.

tests.name: High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hs-CRP)
tests.explanation_low: Low hs-CRP demonstrates minimal systemic arterial inflammation, indicating low baseline cardiovascular risk.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated hs-CRP (>3.0 mg/L) indicates systemic inflammation or heightened cardiovascular risk.

tests.name: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
tests.explanation_low: Low ESR is a normal finding indicating absence of systemic acute-phase inflammatory protein elevation.
tests.explanation_high: High ESR indicates non-specific systemic inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, or tissue injury.

tests.name: Troponin-I
tests.explanation_low: Normal low Troponin-I confirms absence of acute cardiac muscle injury or necrosis.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated Troponin-I is a critical cardiac marker signaling myocardial injury or acute coronary syndrome.

tests.name: Total Testosterone
tests.explanation_low: Low total testosterone can cause fatigue, decreased muscle mass, low libido, and mood shifts.
tests.explanation_high: High total testosterone can be associated with exogenous hormone therapy or endocrine conditions.

tests.name: Free Testosterone
tests.explanation_low: Low free testosterone reflects reduced bioavailable hormone accessible to tissues.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated free testosterone indicates abundant bioavailable hormone levels.

tests.name: Estradiol (E2)
tests.explanation_low: Low estradiol can impact bone density, menstrual regularity, or cardiovascular protection.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated estradiol can lead to fluid retention, gynecomastia in men, or menstrual irregularities.

tests.name: Cortisol
tests.explanation_low: Low morning cortisol can suggest adrenal insufficiency (Addisons disease) or chronic stress burn-out.
tests.explanation_high: High cortisol can reflect acute stress, prolonged glucocorticoid use, or Cushings syndrome.

tests.name: Progesterone
tests.explanation_low: Low progesterone can contribute to irregular menstrual cycles or luteal phase defect.
tests.explanation_high: High progesterone is naturally elevated during ovulation, pregnancy, or progesterone therapy.

tests.name: Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA)
tests.explanation_low: Low PSA indicates healthy prostate gland tissue with minimal tissue clearance into blood.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated PSA can indicate benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prostate inflammation (prostatitis), or prostate tissue changes.

tests.name: Lipase
tests.explanation_low: Low lipase is generally normal but can occasionally occur in chronic pancreatic damage.
tests.explanation_high: Elevated lipase (>3x upper limit) is a key diagnostic indicator of acute pancreatitis or pancreatic duct blockage.

tests.name: Amylase
tests.explanation_low: Low serum amylase can occur in chronic pancreatitis, liver disease, or cystic fibrosis.
tests.explanation_high: High amylase points toward acute pancreatitis, salivary gland inflammation, or abdominal conditions.
